title: The Unexpected Career Killer: Lack of Emotional Intelligence
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that technical excellence has become the baseline for tech professionals, and that stalled careers are often explained by a gap in emotional intelligence. She illustrates with her own path from an early job on a pizza line to analytics, describing how she resisted a mentor's growth-mindset advice until the word assert reframed feedback as a lifeline instead of an attack. She recommends treating feedback as a development resource, using a Stoic split between what you control and what you do not, and building the habit of listening empathically before speaking up. Her closing example is that she spoke up with a hypothesis in a meeting, was asked to investigate it, and later won her first analytics role, with the point that AI could analyse the data but not originate the question. The piece is personal and loosely structured, ending in three one-line takeaways.
points: Technical skill is the expected baseline, so relationship management and the ability to express the value of your work are the differentiators.
Reading feedback as a lifeline instead of an attack, with a Stoic focus on controlling your own response, accelerates growth.
Changing habits is hard work, so building emotional intelligence means practising uncomfortable behaviours such as speaking up early.
Empathic listening first and a tailored contribution second helped the author assert expertise and win a stretch assignment.
What got you here will not get you there, and the constant across her roles was empathy, connection and relationships.
quotes: This is where Stoicism becomes your superpower. The ancient Stoics taught us to distinguish between what we can truly control and what we cannot.
You can't control others' perceptions entirely. You can, though, control your response to feedback.
Developing and growing can be uncomfortable. But, if you want to accelerate in your career, do you expect to stay frozen in your ways?

It was uncomfortable speaking up on the fly in the room. I had to master the habit of forcing myself to do, even going as far as to write a small note in my workbook. I would push myself to speak early, to get it over with.

While AI tools could have helped analyze that data, they couldn't have generated the original hypothesis that came from my human experience and intuition. This is the Human-AI Thought anchor in action – knowing when to leverage technology as your partner while keeping your humanity central to the process.
What got you to point A will not get you to point B. Parts of it will, but not entirely.
